blocks.title: Scalars and vectors
blocks.md: A **scalar** has size only (distance, speed, mass, time). A **vector** has size and **direction** (displacement, velocity, force, acceleration). **Distance** is the length of the path travelled; **displacement** is the straight-line distance from start to finish in a given direction. **Speed** = distance ÷ time; **velocity** = displacement ÷ time, in a stated direction.

items.text: (the time between two dots is always the same)

blocks.caption: Dots made at equal time intervals: steady speed and increasing speed.
blocks.alt: Two rows of dots: the top row evenly spaced, the bottom row with spacing that grows.

blocks.title: Acceleration
blocks.md: **Acceleration** is the rate of change of velocity: **a = (v − u) ÷ t**, where u is the initial velocity, v the final velocity and t the time. Unit: **m/s²**. A **negative** acceleration is a **deceleration** (slowing down). Uniform acceleration means constant acceleration.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Speed and velocity are not the same: a car going round a circuit at 20 m/s has a changing velocity because its direction changes.
- Acceleration is not speed: a body can be fast with zero acceleration.
- Use u for the start and v for the end; do not swap them.

blocks.title: Distance-time graphs
blocks.md: The **gradient** of a distance-time graph is the **speed**. A straight sloping line shows **constant speed**, a steeper line a higher speed, a **horizontal line** an object at rest, and a **curve** a changing speed.

blocks.caption: A velocity-time graph: speeding up, constant speed, slowing down.
blocks.alt: A graph of velocity (m/s) against time (s): a line rising from 0 to 10 m/s in 5 s, flat at 10 m/s until 15 s, then falling to 0 at 20 s.

blocks.title: Velocity-time graphs
blocks.md: On a **velocity-time graph**: the **gradient** is the **acceleration** (a rising line is positive, a falling line negative, a flat line zero acceleration at constant velocity). The **area under the graph** is the **distance travelled**. For the graph above the area is two triangles and a rectangle.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- A horizontal line is **rest** on a distance-time graph but **constant velocity** on a velocity-time graph.
- Read the axes first: the same shape means different things on different graphs.
- Use the scales to get the gradient: rise ÷ run with units.

blocks.title: Equations for uniform acceleration
blocks.md:
For constant acceleration a, starting at velocity u:

**v = u + at**

**s = ½(u + v) t** (distance = average velocity × time)

Signs: take the direction of motion as positive. Both equations come from the velocity-time graph: the first from its gradient, the second from the area of the trapezium.

blocks.title: Free fall
blocks.md: When air resistance is small, **all objects fall with the same acceleration** called the **acceleration of free fall, g**. In this course **g = 10 m/s²** (a more exact value is 9.8 m/s²). A dropped object starts with u = 0, so **v = gt**, and the distance fallen is **h = ½ g t²**. In air, a feather falls slower than a stone because of **air resistance**, not because it is lighter.

blocks.caption: Distance fallen from rest (metres) after 1, 2 and 3 s, with g = 10 m/s².
blocks.alt: A bar chart: 5 m after 1 s, 20 m after 2 s, 45 m after 3 s.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Distance fallen is **not** proportional to time: it grows with t², so in the second second the object falls farther than in the first.
- Weight does not change the acceleration of free fall in a vacuum.
- Remember u = 0 for 'dropped from rest', but not for 'thrown downward'.

blocks.title: Dropped from a height
blocks.statement: A stone is dropped from a bridge 20 m above a river (g = 10 m/s²). Find the time to reach the water and the speed on impact.
steps: h = ½ g t², so 20 = 5 t² and t² = 4, t = 2 s.
